items.prompt: Use unit squares to build rectangles with width 3 units and positive whole-number lengths. List every possible area up to and including 30 square units, and give the matching length. Explain why 28 square units is impossible under these conditions. Then give two possible areas greater than 30 and one other impossible whole-number area.
items.expected_answer: Lengths 1–10 give areas 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30. 28 is not divisible by 3. Examples above 30: 33 and 36. Another impossible example: 31.
items.explanation: For an integer length n, area=3n. The upper bound 3n≤30 gives n≤10, so trying n=1 through 10 accounts for every possible rectangle. 28÷3 leaves remainder 1, so a width of 3 would require a non-integer length. Above 30, every positive multiple of 3 is possible; every positive whole number not divisible by 3 is impossible.

judging_rules: Require all ten areas and corresponding lengths.
Accept any two distinct multiples of 3 above 30 and any additional positive nonmultiple of 3.
Do not require an uploaded drawing; this adaptation assesses a list and explanation.

items.prompt: Find the value of each expression mentally. \(2\times7\) \(4\times7\) \(3\times7\) \(7\times7\)
items.explanation: 2×7=14. Double that result to get 4×7=28. Add one more group of 7 to 2×7 to obtain 3×7=21. Finally 7×7=(4+3)×7=28+21=49. The same factor 7 lets known products support the others.

judging_rules: Check every expression in the stated order; accept equivalent mathematical notation.

items.prompt: The table shows different areas. How many rectangles can be made for each area? Complete the table and be prepared to explain or show your reasoning. Rectangles with the same pair of side lengths should be counted only once. For example, if you count a rectangle with 4 units across and 6 units down, you don’t need to also count a rectangle with 6 units across and 4 units down. area how many rectangles? prime or composite? 2 square units 10 square units 48 square units 11 square units 21 square units 23 square units 60 square units 32 square units 42 square units 31 square units 56 square units
items.expected_answer: 2: 1 rectangle(s), prime; 10: 2 rectangle(s), composite; 48: 5 rectangle(s), composite; 11: 1 rectangle(s), prime; 21: 2 rectangle(s), composite; 23: 1 rectangle(s), prime; 60: 6 rectangle(s), composite; 32: 3 rectangle(s), composite; 42: 4 rectangle(s), composite; 31: 1 rectangle(s), prime; 56: 4 rectangle(s), composite.
items.explanation: Use positive whole-number side lengths and count a rotated rectangle only once. For each area n, test potential shorter sides from 1 through floor(√n); a divisor d gives exactly one pair (d,n/d). The complete pairs are: 2: 1×2; 10: 1×10, 2×5; 48: 1×48, 2×24, 3×16, 4×12, 6×8; 11: 1×11; 21: 1×21, 3×7; 23: 1×23; 60: 1×60, 2×30, 3×20, 4×15, 5×12, 6×10; 32: 1×32, 2×16, 4×8; 42: 1×42, 2×21, 3×14, 6×7; 31: 1×31; 56: 1×56, 2×28, 4×14, 7×8. A prime number greater than 1 has only the pair 1×n; a composite number has another factor pair.

judging_rules: Require all eleven rectangle counts and classifications.
A rotated pair is not an additional rectangle.

items.prompt: Find the value of each expression mentally. \(10 \times 6\) \(3 \times 6\) \(13 \times 6\) \(12 \times 4\)
items.explanation: 10×6=60 and 3×6=18. Split 13 into 10+3: 13×6=60+18=78. Likewise 12×4=(10+2)×4=40+8=48. Distributing the factor over a sum keeps the total number of equal groups unchanged.

judging_rules: Check every expression in the stated order; accept equivalent mathematical notation.

items.prompt: Students are preparing for a party. The school has tables where 6 people can sit and tables where 8 people can sit. The students can only choose one type of table and they want to avoid having empty seats. Jada’s class has 18 students. Which tables would you choose for Jada’s class? Explain or show your reasoning. Noah’s class has 30 students. Which tables would you choose for Noah’s class? Explain or show your reasoning. Which tables would you choose for Noah’s and Jada’s classes together? Can you find more than one option? Explain or show your reasoning. If you also want places for Noah’s teacher and Jada’s teacher to sit, which tables would you choose? Explain or show your reasoning.
items.expected_answer: Jada: three 6-seat tables. Noah: five 6-seat tables. Together: eight 6-seat tables or six 8-seat tables. With two teachers: 50 people; neither table type gives exactly 50 seats. If empty seats are allowed, nine 6-seat tables leave 4 empty seats, or seven 8-seat tables leave 6.
items.explanation: 18 and 30 are divisible by 6 but not by 8, so only 6-seat tables work without empty seats for either class separately. Together 18+30=48 is a common multiple: 48=8×6=6×8. Adding two teachers gives 50, which is divisible by neither 6 nor 8. Under the original no-empty-seat condition there is no solution; relaxing that condition requires rounding table counts upward, not discarding the extra people.

judging_rules: Final part must recognize that exact seating is impossible under the no-empty-seat condition.
Do not mark an answer wrong merely for refusing to choose an impossible exact table arrangement.

items.prompt: Each package of hot dogs has 10 hot dogs. Each package of hot dog buns has 8 buns. Lin expects to need 50 hot dogs for a class picnic. How many packages of hot dogs should Lin get? Explain or show your reasoning. Can Lin get exactly 50 hot dog buns? How many packages of hot dog buns should Lin get? Explain or show your reasoning. Diego expects to need 72 hot dogs for a class picnic. How many packages of hot dogs should Diego get? Explain or show your reasoning. How many packages of hot dog buns should Diego get? Explain or show your reasoning. Is it possible to buy exactly the same number of hot dogs and buns? If you think so, what would that number be? If not, explain your reasoning.
items.expected_answer: Lin: 5 hot-dog packages; exactly 50 buns is impossible, so at least 7 bun packages (56 buns). Diego: at least 8 hot-dog packages (80 hot dogs) and 9 bun packages (72 buns). Equal totals are possible, for example 40 of each (4 hot-dog packages and 5 bun packages).
items.explanation: Divide the required quantity by the pack size and round upward when there is a remainder. For 50 hot dogs, 50÷10=5; for 50 buns, 6 packs supply only 48, so buy 7. For 72 hot dogs, 7 packs supply only 70, so buy 8; 72 buns fit exactly into 9 packs. A total that can be bought exactly as both hot dogs and buns must be divisible by both 10 and 8. Their least positive common multiple is 40; any positive multiple of 40 is also valid.

judging_rules: Accept any positive multiple of 40 for the final equal-total example.
Keep Diego’s minimum purchases distinct from the separate equal-total question.

items.prompt: The 20 students in Tyler’s fourth-grade class are playing a game in a hallway with 20 lockers in a row. Your goal is to find out which lockers will be touched as all 20 students take their turn touching lockers. Which locker numbers does the 3rd student touch? Which locker numbers does the 5th student touch? How many students touch locker 17? Explain or show how you know. Which lockers are only touched by 2 students? Explain or show how you know. Which lockers are touched by only 3 students? Explain or show how you know. Which lockers are touched the most? Explain or show how you know. If you have time: Which lockers are still open at the end of the game? Explain or show how you know.
items.expected_answer: Student 3: 3,6,9,12,15,18. Student 5: 5,10,15,20. Locker 17: two students (1 and 17). Exactly two touches: 2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19. Exactly three touches: 4,9. Most touches: 12,18,20, each six times. Optional final answer: 1,4,9,16 remain open.
items.explanation: Student d touches exactly the locker numbers divisible by d. Therefore a locker n is touched once for each positive divisor of n. Primes have two divisors. 4 has divisors 1,2,4 and 9 has 1,3,9. The complete divisor counts for 1–20 show a maximum of six for 12,18,20. All lockers start closed and every touch toggles the state, so an odd number of divisors leaves a locker open. Divisors pair as d and n/d except at a square root, so precisely the perfect squares 1,4,9,16 stay open.

judging_rules: The last subquestion is optional as stated in the source; do not penalize omission.
Require reasoning that connects touches to divisors, not only the final lists.

items.prompt: For each number 10, 7, 50, 16, 35, 20, 19, and 6, write one true statement using “factor” and one true statement using “multiple”. Each pair of statements must include the given number. Give a multiplication equation to justify each statement. Use positive whole numbers. Many answers are possible.
items.expected_answer: One valid set uses 1×n=n for each given n: “1 is a factor of n” and “n is a multiple of 1.” More informative examples include: 2 is a factor of 10 and 10 is a multiple of 2 (2×5=10); 7 is a factor of 35 and 35 is a multiple of 7 (7×5=35).
items.explanation: A positive whole number d is a factor of n exactly when n=d×k for a positive whole number k. The same equation says n is a multiple of d. To check each sentence, translate it to multiplication and confirm that one of the numbers is the required number. There is no unique list: for instance, 7 is a factor of 14 and 14 is a multiple of 7 are both valid statements for the given number 7. Do not reverse the relation without checking divisibility.

judging_rules: Accept every mathematically valid pair for each of the eight given numbers, not just sample wording.
Require a supporting multiplication equality; 1 and the number itself are valid factors.
Partner discussion is removed in this independent written adaptation.

items.prompt: Find the value of each expression mentally. \(12 \div 3\) \(30 \div 3\) \(60 \div 3\) \(72 \div 3\)
items.explanation: 12÷3=4 because 3×4=12. 30÷3=10 and 60÷3=20. Split 72 into 60+12: 72÷3=20+4=24. Check each quotient by multiplying it by the divisor 3.

judging_rules: Check every expression in the stated order; accept equivalent mathematical notation.
